---
title: "Control Flow in Rust"
---

Rust's control flow looks familiar if you know C#, Dart, or Python, but one design decision changes how you use it: **almost everything is an expression**. `if`, `match`, `loop`, and even plain `{ }` blocks produce values. Most of the other differences follow from that.

## 0. The core idea: expressions and the semicolon rule

```
 Statement-oriented (C#/Java style)     Expression-oriented (Rust)
 ──────────────────────────────────     ─────────────────────────────────
 int x;                                 let x = if ok { 1 } else { 2 };
 if (ok) { x = 1; } else { x = 2; }             └──── yields a value ────┘
```

A block evaluates to its **last expression**, as long as that expression has **no trailing semicolon**:

```rust
let a = { let t = 2; t * 10 };   // a = 20
let b = { let t = 2; t * 10; };  // b = ()  ← the semicolon turned it into a statement
```

```
 { stmt; stmt; expr }   →  value of expr
 { stmt; stmt; expr; }  →  ()   ("unit", Rust's "nothing" value)
```

This is also how functions return values without writing `return`.

---

## 1. `if` / `else if` / `else`

```rust
let temp = 38.2;

if temp >= 39.0 {
    println!("high fever");
} else if temp >= 37.5 {
    println!("fever");
} else {
    println!("normal");
}
```

There are three differences from what you may be used to. First, there are **no parentheses** around the condition, but **braces are mandatory**, even for one line. Second, the condition **must be a `bool`**. Rust has no truthiness, so `if 1 { }`, `if some_vec { }`, and `if some_string { }` are compile errors. Python, JS, and R all allow these, so this one tends to catch people. You write `if !v.is_empty()` instead. Third, `if` is an expression, so it replaces the ternary operator:

```rust
let label = if temp >= 37.5 { "fever" } else { "normal" };
```

Both arms must have **the same type**. `if x { 5 } else { "five" }` is a compile error.

---

## 2. Loops: `loop`, `while`, `for`

```
 loop   ──► repeat forever until `break` (can return a value)
 while  ──► repeat while a bool condition is true
 for    ──► iterate over anything that implements IntoIterator
```

### `loop`: an infinite loop that can return a value

```rust
let mut attempts = 0;

let result = loop {
    attempts += 1;
    if attempts == 3 {
        break attempts * 10;   // `break` carries a value out of the loop
    }
};
// result == 30
```

This works well for retry logic: keep trying, and break out with the successful value.

### `while`

```rust
let mut n = 3;
while n > 0 {
    println!("{n}...");
    n -= 1;
}
println!("liftoff!");
```

### `for`: the one you'll use most

```rust
for i in 0..5    { }   // 0,1,2,3,4      (exclusive end)
for i in 0..=5   { }   // 0,1,2,3,4,5    (inclusive end)
for i in (0..5).rev() { }   // 4,3,2,1,0

let names = vec!["Ann", "Bo", "Cy"];
for (i, name) in names.iter().enumerate() {
    println!("{i}: {name}");
}
```

Rust has no C-style `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)`. Writing `for i in 0..v.len() { v[i] }` is legal but not idiomatic. The usual approach is to iterate the collection directly, which avoids bounds checks and off-by-one bugs.

**The ownership twist.** How you write the `for` decides what happens to the collection:

```
 for x in v         x: T        v is MOVED (consumed), unusable afterwards
 for x in &v        x: &T       borrow, read-only     (same as v.iter())
 for x in &mut v    x: &mut T   borrow, can modify    (same as v.iter_mut())
```

```rust
let mut scores = vec![1, 2, 3];
for s in &mut scores { *s *= 10; }   // scores = [10, 20, 30]
for s in &scores { println!("{s}"); }
for s in scores { /* takes ownership */ }
// println!("{:?}", scores);  ❌ error: value moved
```

### Loop labels for nested loops

```rust
'outer: for i in 0..5 {
    for j in 0..5 {
        if i * j == 6 {
            println!("found {i} x {j}");
            break 'outer;          // exits BOTH loops
        }
    }
}
```

The leading apostrophe marks a label. These are not lifetimes, even though they share the syntax.

---

## 3. `match`: Rust's most important control-flow tool

`match` is like `switch`, but it compares against **patterns**, and the compiler requires it to be **exhaustive**. If you forget a case, the code won't compile.

```rust
fn describe(n: i32) -> &'static str {
    match n {
        0               => "zero",
        1 | 2 | 3       => "small",          // OR-pattern
        4..=9           => "medium",         // range pattern
        x if x < 0      => "negative",       // match guard
        _               => "large",          // wildcard: "everything else"
    }
}
```

```
 value ──► arm 1? ──no──► arm 2? ──no──► ... ──► _ (catch-all)
              │yes           │yes
              ▼              ▼
           result         result        ← first matching arm wins (top to bottom)
```

### Destructuring enums

This is where `match` earns its place:

```rust
enum Shape {
    Circle { r: f64 },
    Rect { w: f64, h: f64 },
    Point,
}

fn area(s: &Shape) -> f64 {
    match s {
        Shape::Circle { r }  => std::f64::consts::PI * r * r,
        Shape::Rect { w, h } => w * h,
        Shape::Point         => 0.0,
    }
}
```

If you later add `Shape::Triangle` to the enum, every `match` that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error (`E0004: non-exhaustive patterns`). The compiler gives you a list of places to update. C#'s switch expressions and Dart 3's sealed classes offer something similar, but in Rust it is enforced everywhere by default.

### Matching on tuples

```rust
match (is_urgent, is_complete) {
    (true, false) => "do it now",
    (_, true)     => "done",
    (false, false)=> "later",
}
```

---

## 4. Shorthand for one pattern: `if let`, `let else`, `while let`

A full `match` is verbose when you only care about one case. That situation comes up all the time with `Option` and `Result`.

```rust
let maybe_id: Option<u32> = Some(42);

// Full match
match maybe_id {
    Some(id) => println!("id = {id}"),
    None => {}
}

// if let: "if it matches this pattern, bind and run"
if let Some(id) = maybe_id {
    println!("id = {id}");
} else {
    println!("no id");
}
```

**`let else`** is for the "unwrap or bail out" guard pattern, and it keeps the happy path unindented:

```rust
fn parse_port(s: &str) -> u16 {
    let Ok(port) = s.parse::<u16>() else {
        return 8080;          // else-block MUST diverge (return/break/continue/panic)
    };
    port                      // `port` is in scope here, already unwrapped
}
```

**`while let`** loops for as long as the pattern keeps matching:

```rust
let mut stack = vec![1, 2, 3];
while let Some(top) = stack.pop() {
    println!("{top}");        // 3, 2, 1 — stops when pop() returns None
}
```

In the **Rust 2024 edition** you can also chain conditions with `&&`: `if let Some(x) = opt && x > 5 { ... }`.

---

## 5. Early exit with `?`

`?` is control flow too. On `Err` or `None`, it **returns early** from the current function. On success, it unwraps the value.

```rust
fn double_input(s: &str) -> Result<i32, std::num::ParseIntError> {
    let n = s.trim().parse::<i32>()?;   // Err → return Err(...) immediately
    Ok(n * 2)
}
```

```
 s.parse()?
     │
     ├── Ok(v)  ──► v continues down the function
     └── Err(e) ──► return Err(e) from the function right now
```

You'll see this constantly. It's how Rust gets exception-like ergonomics without having exceptions.

---

## 6. A bonus insight: the "never" type `!`

How can this type-check, when one arm is an `i32` and the other is a `return`?

```rust
let n: i32 = match maybe_n {
    Some(v) => v,
    None => return,     // ← what type is this?
};
```

`return`, `break`, `continue`, and `panic!()` have the type `!` ("never"), because they never produce a value. The compiler knows `!` can stand in for any type, so the arms agree. The same rule is why the `else` block in `let else` must diverge.

---

## Cheat sheet: which construct to use?

```
 Need to BRANCH?
  ├─ on a bool ............................ if / else
  ├─ on the shape/variant of a value ...... match
  │    └─ only care about one pattern ..... if let  /  let ... else
 Need to REPEAT?
  ├─ over a collection or range ........... for
  ├─ while a condition holds .............. while
  ├─ while a pattern keeps matching ....... while let
  └─ forever / retry + return a value ..... loop  (break value)
 Need to BAIL OUT early?
  └─ on Err / None ........................ ?
```

## Common beginner gotchas

The most frequent surprise is a **stray semicolon** on the last line of a block or function. It turns your value into `()`, and you get a "mismatched types: expected `i32`, found `()`" error. The second is **mismatched arm types** in `if` or `match` used as expressions. The third is expecting **truthiness**: always compare explicitly, as in `!v.is_empty()` or `x != 0`. The last is **moving a collection with `for x in v`** when you meant to borrow with `&v`.
